To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) reliable and unreliable partisan appointee Governors to the Board of Gover-nors exist; (2) reliable Governors are more likely to be appointed early in a Presidential term, when the returns from influencing monetary policy are high; (3) unreliable Governors are more likely be appointed late in a Presidential term when the returns from interest group support are important; and (4) the background of the Governors, particularly whether they are economists or not, influences whether or not they are reliable.

the Board of Governors is a highly politicized body, that it is a body that has a history of partisan appointments, and that the partisan voting behavior of Governors has changed over the years in a manner that is consistent with the partisan nature of the appointing administration.

the partisan voting behavior of Federal Reserve Board members is a function of their background and that partisan voting behavior is a consequence of the political process that appoints Board members.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the political economy of Federal Reserve decision-making.
the question of whether or not the Federal Reserve System has been captured by special interests, and if so, what the implications are for the conduct of monetary policy.
the political economy of Federal Reserve appointments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Fed has been a political creature, but not in the sense that its actions can be explained in terms of the political preferences of its agents.
the Fed is a political institution that is not averse to using its power to achieve its own goals, but is constrained by political and economic forces.
the Federal Reserve is a complex and evolving institution whose behavior is determined by the interplay of a number of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Federal Reserve System is not a unitary decision-making institution.

, in a political economy framework, a rational expectations model of the Federal Reserve would be a model that features the interaction of multiple agents, with the Federal Reserve as the central agent.
the Federal Reserve is a complex, dynamic, and evolving organization that is not easily characterized as either independent or dependent on the President.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Board of Governors is not a unitary actor but a collection of individual actors whose behavior is not fully determined by the President who appoints them.
, contrary to the rational expectations game-theoretic approach, the Federal Reserve’s policy making process is not the result of a single principal’s attempt to maximize his utility function.
the Federal Reserve is not the unitary actor that the rational expectations — game theoretic models portray.
